newsitem.title: USA: MCA prepares to meet Wall Street.
newsitem.headline: MCA prepares to meet Wall Street.

text.p: Wall Street will get its first look at MCA Inc's new management team on Tuesday when senior executives from Seagram Co Ltd's MCA offer their script for vaulting the beverage and entertainment company into Hollywood's top tier.

Billed as the first detailed meeting with analysts since Seagram Co Ltd acquired MCA more than a year ago, the session is expected to feature presentations on both of Seagram's major businesses -- beverage and entertainment.
The meeting is expected to attract more than 200 analysts.
Among the issues analysts will be seeking information about are Seagram's plans for revitalizing its MCA film, music and television operations.
Seagram acquired an 80 percent stake in MCA in June 1995 for $5.7 billion in an effort to diversify beyond its core beverage operations.

Since then, Seagram Chief Executive Officer Edgar Bronfman has been busy filling key executive slots, including former Viacom Inc chief Frank Biondi, talent agent Ron Meyer and ex-Time Warner Inc music boss Doug Morris.
MCA executives say their goal is to increase profitability at the studio and become one of the leading providers of music, film, theme parks and television programming.

"We are in the process of trying to impose a growth culture on top of a 75-year legacy that we've inherited," MCA Chairman and Chief Executive Frank Biondi said recently. "We have not been a grower in terms of operating income or EBITDA. We're going to change that."
EBITDA is earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization.

"We're literally re-inventing the company," he said. "Our essential goal is really to become a faster, more flexible, more customer-responsive organization. We're also going to try to create a brand for the customer and we're going to base it around the theme of the magic of Hollywood."
Such promises have been made before by MCA, only to be forgotten as the pressures of churning out blockbusters quickly overwhelmed financial targets.
In 1995, the studio spent an estimated $200 million on the futuristic thriller "Waterworld", only to watch it drown at the box office.
While MCA's former owner Matsushita Electric Industrial bore the brunt of the Waterworld costs, MCA executives say Bronfman has set high standards for performance.

"The Bronfmans have high expectations," MCA Television Group Chairman Greg Meidel said in a recent interview. "They didn't bring in a new management team to be status quo and every one of us has been changed," he said.
